clinical_knowledge.topic: First-Episode Psychosis / Schizophrenia evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of First-Episode Psychosis / Schizophrenia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes urgent psychiatric admission for safety and diagnostic evaluation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: acute auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, and disorganized behavior over 2 months

Key HPI features: 24M college student brought by campus security after barricading himself in his dorm room for 5 days. Claims the FBI has implanted a microchip in his dental filling to broadcast his thoughts and monitor his actions. Reports hearing two distinct voices commanding him to smash his computer. Has stopped attending classes, neglected personal hygiene, and shows flat affect with formal thought disorder (derailment).

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 88, BP 124/80. Patient is unkempt, malodorous, with suspicious guarded posture and poor eye contact. Speech is fluent but exhibits loose associations and tangentiality. Affect is blunted and incongruent. Endorses third-person commanding auditory hallucinations and thought broadcasting. Cognitive orientation intact. Urine drug screen negative for amphetamines/cocaine, positive for cannabinoids. Comprehensive lab workup (TSH, RPR, B12, CMP) and head CT unremarkable, ruling out organic secondary causes.
Relevant background/PMH: No prior psychiatric history; cannabis use socially
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out First-Episode Psychosis / Schizophrenia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Bipolar I with psychotic features without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Command auditory hallucinations.
management_principles: Urgently admit to an acute psychiatric inpatient unit; maintain observation and assess risk to self or others, including whether command hallucinations are actionable
After psychiatric assessment, consider a second-generation antipsychotic with baseline and ongoing metabolic, neurologic, and other indicated monitoring
Provide low-stimulus environment and supportive reality-oriented nursing care
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 24M first-episode presentation of psychosis characterized by persecutory/passivity delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, and negative symptoms lasting >1 month.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 88, BP 124/80. Patient is unkempt, malodorous, with suspicious guarded posture and poor eye contact. Speech is fluent but exhibits loose associations and tangentiality. Affect is blunted and incongruent. Endorses third-person commanding auditory hallucinations and thought broadcasting. Cognitive orientation intact. Urine drug screen negative for amphetamines/cocaine, positive for cannabinoids. Comprehensive lab workup (TSH, RPR, B12, CMP) and head CT unremarkable, ruling out organic secondary causes.
reference_soap.assessment: First-Episode Psychosis, schizophreniform disorder vs Schizophrenia (meeting DSM-5 Criterion A symptoms with duration >1 month and marked functional impairment).
reference_soap.plan: Urgently admit to an acute psychiatric inpatient unit for safety and diagnostic evaluation, with observation and assessment of risk to self or others, including whether command hallucinations are actionable. After psychiatric assessment, consider a second-generation antipsychotic with baseline and ongoing metabolic, neurologic, and other indicated monitoring. Provide a low-stimulus environment and supportive reality-oriented nursing care. Obtain collateral and capacity assessment as clinically indicated; involve social work for family psychoeducation and referral to an early-intervention psychosis program.

learning_objectives: Perform a structured mental status examination assessing for formal thought disorder, delusions, and perceptual disturbances
Differentiate primary psychotic disorders (Schizophrenia/Schizophreniform) from substance-induced psychosis and organic medical conditions
Select first-line second-generation antipsychotic pharmacotherapy and monitor for extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and metabolic side effects
Outline principles of early intervention and family psychoeducation in first-episode psychosis

teaching.one_liner: Psychotic disorder characterized by delusions, auditory hallucinations, disorganized thought processes, and negative symptoms.
red_flags: Severe paranoia with threat to self/others
Suicidal thoughts, intent, plan, or access to means
Violent thoughts, intent, or inability to resist harmful commands

must_ask.say: Do you hear voices or sounds that other people around you cannot hear?
Do you feel that people are watching, spying, or trying to harm you?
Do you ever feel like your mind is being broadcasted aloud or controlled by outside forces?
Have you been using cannabis, amphetamines, or hallucinogens recently?
Have you isolated yourself from friends or stopped attending work or school?
Have the voices told you to hurt yourself or anyone else, and do you feel you might act on that?

history.answer: He has been hearing strange voices and saying bizarre things for a couple of months, and campus security had to bring him in after he barricaded himself in his dorm.
His personality began changing gradually about two months ago, but his strange behavior became much worse over the past five days.
He told us he hears two distinct voices talking about him and commenting on his actions throughout the day.
He has never mentioned seeing visions, shadows, or anything that was not actually there.
He said the voices were commanding him to smash his computer because it was sending out information.
He insists that the FBI placed a microchip inside his dental filling to track his movements and monitor his actions.
He claims that his private thoughts are being broadcast out loud so everyone around him can hear them.
He barricaded his dorm room door for five straight days, stopped taking showers, and hasn't changed his clothes.
He completely stopped going to his college classes and cut off all contact with his friends over the last month.
No, he hasn't been euphoric or speaking with pressured speech, although his thoughts wander tangentially from topic to topic.
No, he hasn't been reckless with spending money, gambling, driving fast, or engaging in risky behaviors.
No, he has never had any episodes of severe depression or prolonged low mood in the past.
The voices and beliefs have been present every single day, regardless of how his mood is.
He has never expressed any thoughts of wanting to die or harm himself, and we haven't seen any self-harm.
He smashed his laptop because the voices ordered him to, but he has never attacked anyone or carried a weapon.
He insists there is nothing wrong with his mind and refuses to accept that he needs psychiatric treatment.
He believes this entire hospital is secretly part of a government surveillance network set up to monitor him.
He is terrified that the voices will punish him severely if he talks to the doctors or cooperates with staff.
He is desperately demanding his phone back so he can post online and expose the government conspiracy.
He smokes marijuana socially with college friends, but he has never touched methamphetamines, cocaine, or any other hard drugs.
No, he hasn't had any fevers, headaches, seizures, body tremors, palpitations, or unexplained weight loss.
He has barely slept over the past five days while locked in his room, but there was no major life crisis right before this began.
He has never been diagnosed with any chronic medical illnesses and has always been physically healthy.
He has never had any operations and has never been admitted to a hospital before.
He does not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or dietary supplements.
He has never been prescribed or taken any psychiatric medications like mood stabilizers or antipsychotics.
He has no known allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
No, he has never smoked cigarettes or used any vaping products.
He occasionally drinks a beer or two on weekends, but he does not drink heavily and has never had alcohol withdrawal.
He is a 24-year-old college senior and has been living alone in an on-campus dormitory room.
There is no family history of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, severe depression, or suicide on either side.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 124/80 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
He appears unkempt and malodorous with a guarded, suspicious posture, frequently scanning the room and avoiding eye contact.
He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time, but demonstrates a blunted affect, tangential speech with loose associations, persecutory delusions, thought broadcasting, and absent insight.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light with intact extraocular movements and no nystagmus or scleral icterus.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, and without palpable nodules or bruits.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial expressions and no focal deficit.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 strength throughout all four extremities and no involuntary movements.
Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally with downgoing plantar reflexes.
Normal finger-to-nose testing, steady unassisted gait, and a negative Romberg sign.
Supple neck with no nuchal rigidity, Kernig sign, or Brudzinski sign.
